Fathers’ Rights and Parenting Plans in Washington: What the Statute Actually Asks

7 min read·Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law

You have been served, or you are about to file, and the question underneath every other question is whether a Washington court is going to treat you as the backup parent. Search for fathers’ rights in Washington state and you will mostly find grievance rather than law. The statute Washington judges actually apply is written down, it is gender-neutral on its face, and knowing what it weighs changes how you approach your own case.

Washington does not use the word “custody”

Washington replaced custody and visitation with a single governing document called a parenting plan. Under RCW 26.09.184, a permanent parenting plan must contain a residential schedule saying where each child lives on given days of the year, an allocation of decision-making authority over education, health care, and religious upbringing, and a process for resolving future disputes short of returning to court. Those three pieces move independently, so a parent can have fewer overnights and still hold joint decision-making, and people sign plans whose schedule looks tolerable without noticing what the decision-making paragraph did.

Does Washington law favor mothers?

Nothing in chapter 26.09 RCW assigns a preference to either parent based on gender. RCW 26.09.002 makes the best interests of the child the standard and says that “the relationship between the child and each parent should be fostered unless inconsistent with the child’s best interests.”

Even so, the real asymmetry comes from the list of factors rather than from any preference in the text. RCW 26.09.187(3)(a) gives the court seven factors for the residential schedule and then adds one sentence that does more work than anything else in the chapter: “Factor (i) shall be given the greatest weight.” Factor (i) is the relative strength, nature, and stability of the child’s relationship with each parent, and factor (iii) asks whether a parent “has taken greater responsibility for performing parenting functions relating to the daily needs of the child.” Those functions, defined at RCW 26.09.004(2), are mundane on purpose: feeding, clothing, supervision, health care, day care, education. A father who did those things and can show it is arguing inside the statute, while a father arguing about how unfair the other parent has been is arguing about something the statute never asks.

When the court must limit a parent’s time

Washington has a dedicated restrictions statute, and the Legislature substantially rewrote it in 2025. RCW 26.09.191 separates conduct that requires the court to limit a parent’s residential time from conduct that may lead to limits. The mandatory category includes willful abandonment, physical abuse or a pattern of emotional abuse of a child, a history of acts of domestic violence as defined in RCW 7.105.010, an assault causing grievous bodily harm or the fear of it, and any sexual assault, with sexual abuse of a child now handled under RCW 26.09.192. The discretionary category reaches more ordinary cases, including substantial nonperformance of parenting functions, long-term impairment from substance abuse, abusive use of conflict, and withholding a child from the other parent for a protracted period without good cause.

If you were never married to the mother, parentage comes first

This is the most consequential point on this page and the one I see missed most often. A court cannot enter a residential schedule for a father whose parentage has not been established, and being on the birth certificate, paying for things, living with the child, and being universally known as the dad are not the same thing as a legal parent-child relationship. RCW 26.26A.100 lists how that relationship arises, including a statutory presumption, a signed acknowledgment, an adjudication, and adoption.

The presumptions at RCW 26.26A.115 mostly run through marriage or a state registered domestic partnership, which is why unmarried fathers fall outside them. One does not: a person who “resided in the same household with the child for the first four years of the life of the child” and “openly held out the child as the individual’s child” is presumed to be a parent. Short of that, an unmarried father relies on an acknowledgment of parentage under RCW 26.26A.200 or an adjudication under RCW 26.26A.400.

What follows from that is the part that hurts. A father who never established parentage has no order to enforce when the other parent decides he is not seeing the child this weekend, so parentage is the foundation and everything else waits on it.

The temporary order shapes the case more than people expect

The statute tells the court to disregard the temporary plan when it writes the permanent one. RCW 26.09.191(2)(a) says the court “shall not draw any presumptions from the provisions of the temporary parenting plan.” That rule is real, and it is not the same as saying the temporary schedule does not matter, because RCW 26.09.002 also provides that a child’s best interest is ordinarily served when the existing pattern of interaction between parent and child is altered only as far as the changed relationship of the parents requires, and a temporary schedule that runs a year becomes that existing pattern.

Correspondingly, the motion setting that schedule is governed by RCW 26.09.194, and the required declaration tells you exactly what the court cares about: where the child has lived for the preceding twelve months, each parent’s performance during those twelve months of the parenting functions relating to the child’s daily needs, and both parents’ work and child-care schedules. Fathers who have that record rarely realize it, and fathers who do not rarely start building it until the hearing is a week out.

Child support is a separate calculation, and more time does not automatically lower it

The economic table at RCW 26.19.020 sets a presumptive monthly obligation by combined monthly net income and number of children, and RCW 26.19.035 requires worksheets on the official statewide form, signed under penalty of perjury. RCW 26.19.075(1)(d) does let the court deviate downward when the child spends a significant amount of time with the paying parent, but the deviation is discretionary, and the court may not grant it if doing so would leave insufficient funds in the receiving household to meet the child’s basic needs. Trading residential time for a lower support number is a strategy that frequently produces neither.

After a plan is entered, changing it is harder

Changing a parenting plan is a different proceeding with a deliberately high threshold. RCW 26.09.260 requires facts that arose since the prior plan or were unknown to the court, a substantial change in circumstances, and a modification necessary to serve the child’s best interests. RCW 26.09.270 then directs the court to deny the motion unless adequate cause for a hearing is established by the affidavits, and many petitions die there on the papers without anyone reaching the merits.

Separately, moving with a child runs on its own statute. Under the Child Relocation Act at RCW 26.09.405 through 26.09.560, RCW 26.09.440 requires sixty days’ advance notice in the ordinary case and a warning that the move will be permitted unless an objection is filed and served within thirty days. Most people also have the standard backward, because RCW 26.09.520 creates a rebuttable presumption that the relocation will be permitted and puts the burden on the objecting parent to show that the detrimental effect outweighs the benefit, across eleven unweighted factors.

Where fathers’ cases go wrong

Self-help instead of a motion. A father who believes something is wrong at the other house, and responds by keeping the child or departing from the schedule, has created the clearest fact in the case, and it is a fact about him. Withholding a child for a protracted period without good cause is listed in RCW 26.09.191 as a basis for restricting residential time, and RCW 26.09.260 makes two contempt findings in three years a route to modifying the plan against him. The merits of the original concern do not rescue the method, because the remedy is a motion heard by the court and never a decision made in a driveway.

Agreeing to a temporary plan to keep the peace. A parent who accepts less temporarily, meaning to fix it at trial, ends up explaining at trial why the arrangement he agreed to should change.

Never establishing parentage. Years of being the father in every practical sense, and no order, until the first conflict exposes it.

Informal arrangements never entered as an order. Two cooperative parents work out a schedule and never put it in a plan, and it holds until one of them moves, remarries, or hires a lawyer.

Text messages and social media. Everything you write becomes an exhibit, and a parent’s own messages are often where the proof of abusive use of conflict comes from.

What a lawyer does here that the forms cannot

The Administrative Office of the Courts publishes mandatory pattern forms for all of this, free and public, and the forms are the easy part. Filling one in feels like completing a task, and it will accept almost anything you write on it. What the form does not do is tell you which of the seven residential factors your facts actually reach, how to compress twelve months of daily parenting into a declaration a commissioner reads in four minutes, or whether your facts support a restriction or expose you to one. Practice is local too, since Spokane County Superior Court has its own family law calendar, its own commissioners, and its own expectations about what a motion looks like.

About my practice

I am Justin D. Leigh, an independent attorney in downtown Spokane. In family law I handle parenting plans, parentage, child support, modifications, relocation objections, and the restriction findings under RCW 26.09.191 that often decide the rest of the case, and I appear in superior courts across Washington, most often in Spokane, Klickitat, Kittitas, Benton, Franklin and Yakima counties. I am admitted in Washington (WSBA #55307) and Oregon (OSB #242384), which matters here, because a parenting plan with a household on each side of the Columbia raises questions about which state decides and enforces.

If you want to talk about your own situation

I offer a free initial consultation by appointment at my downtown Spokane office. If you are holding a petition, a relocation notice, or a parenting plan someone wants you to sign, bring the paperwork and a calendar of the last year.
